## Simple explanation

A graph neural network (GNN) processes data represented as nodes and
edges. It uses relationships between entities as well as their
individual features to make predictions.

## Technical explanation

Many GNNs update node representations by aggregating messages from
neighbouring nodes and combining them with the current representation.
After several layers, a node representation can encode information from
multiple graph hops. Architectures differ in aggregation, normalization,
attention, and graph-level pooling.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Graphs represent relationships in social networks, molecules,
transactions, knowledge bases, and infrastructure. GNNs can use this
structure, but require careful handling of scale, dynamic edges,
heterogeneous entities, and train/test leakage through graph connections.

## How it works

Each layer sends or computes messages between connected nodes, aggregates
neighbour information, and updates node embeddings. A prediction head
then uses node, edge, or pooled graph representations for the target
task.

## Practical example

A molecular-property model can represent atoms as nodes and chemical
bonds as edges. A GNN aggregates information through the molecular graph
before predicting a property.

## Common misconceptions

- A GNN does not automatically understand every relationship encoded in
  a graph.
- More message-passing layers can cause oversmoothing or increase cost.
- Graph connectivity and feature construction can introduce leakage if
  they use information unavailable at prediction time.
